title: Understanding the Constitutional Amendment Process in Brazil
subtitle: A comprehensive guide to the legislative process, requirements, and limitations of changing the Brazilian Constitution
excerpt: Learn who can propose, how proposals circulate in Congress, and the barriers to altering the Brazilian Constitution.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The country's foundational text governing political, economic, and social life is not immutable. The 1988 Constitution can be amended, but the path to change is rigorous, designed to ensure stability and prevent impulsive alterations. This article simplifies the trajectory of a constitutional amendment, from its origin to promulgation, and explains what this means for Brazilian citizens.

Who can propose a constitutional amendment?

Article 60 of the Constitution establishes three entities authorized to initiate the process:

  • One-third of the members of the Chamber of Deputies or the Federal Senate;
  • The President of the Republic;
  • More than half of the State Legislative Assemblies, meeting in joint session.

These sources reflect the principle that changes of such magnitude require broad institutional support, preventing a single political agent from dictating alterations to the social pact.

Formal requirements for the proposal

Before being scheduled, the proposal must meet formal requirements:

  • Be presented in writing and numbered, clearly indicating the article or section to be amended;
  • Bear the signature of the authorized entity presenting it;
  • Respect the so-called cláusulas pétreas (petrified clauses), which are provisions that cannot be modified, such as the federal form of state, direct, secret, universal, and periodic voting, separation of powers, and individual rights and guarantees.

If the proposal violates any petrified clause, it is immediately rejected by the President of the Chamber or Senate, even before discussion begins.

Legislative process: two houses, two rounds

The path of the amendment follows a bicameral and bifasic rite:

  1. Presentation and preliminary reading. The proposal is distributed to the thematic committees of the House where it was presented for evaluation of constitutionality and relevance.
  2. Discussion and voting in two rounds. Each house – Chamber of Deputies and Federal Senate – must deliberate on the proposal in two rounds of voting, requiring, in each round, the support of at least three-fifths of the members present.
  3. Approval in both houses. If the first house approves the amendment, the text proceeds to the second house, which repeats the procedure of two votes. If the second house makes changes, the text returns to the first house for new analysis.
  4. Promulgation and publication. Once approved in both houses, the amendment is promulgated by the President of the Republic and published in the Official Gazette, coming into effect immediately, unless otherwise provided.

The requirement of three-fifths of the votes in each round, in both houses, ensures that only proposals with broad political consensus reach the Constitution.

Material limitations: the petrified clauses

Even if all formalities are met, a proposal can be barred for violating the petrified clauses. These are fundamental principles that the Constitution protects against alteration, such as:

  • Individual rights and guarantees (articles 5 to 17);
  • The federal form of state (article 1, items I to IV);
  • Direct, secret, universal, and periodic voting (article 14);
  • Separation of powers (article 2).

Any attempt to modify these provisions is considered unconstitutional and may be annulled by the Federal Supreme Court.

Practical implications for citizens

For Brazilians, understanding the constitutional amendment process has tangible consequences:

  • Informed political participation. Knowing who has the power to propose and what the stages are allows citizens to follow debates and exert pressure on representatives.
  • Legal stability. The rigor of the rite prevents frequent changes that could generate insecurity in contracts, investments, and social rights.
  • Protection of fundamental rights. The petrified clauses function as a shield that prevents setbacks in sensitive areas, such as freedom of expression and equality before the law.

Furthermore, the need for a qualified majority creates incentives for negotiation and consensus, requiring parliamentarians to build alliances before advancing with constitutional changes.

Conclusion: a responsible mechanism for change

The constitutional amendment process in Brazil was designed to balance the need for normative evolution with the preservation of institutional order. By requiring the support of three-fifths of parliamentarians in two houses and protecting petrified clauses, the Constitution creates a path that only allows changes backed by broad consensus and that do not threaten the fundamental principles of the democratic state of law. This framework guarantees that, when the Constitution is effectively altered, society can trust that the transformation was the result of a solid, transparent, and representative debate.
